jurisdictions.note: Capacity, attorney, deputy, succession, disposal of remains and organ donation law for England and Wales, as in force on 2026-09-16. Differences between England and Wales (organ donation) are noted.
jurisdictions.label: UK — England & Wales

jurisdictions.name: Northern Ireland
jurisdictions.note: Northern Ireland roles for incapacity, death and estate administration, as in force on 2026-09-16. UK-wide roles (DWP appointees, UK GDPR) are in the uk-national layer.
jurisdictions.label: UK — Northern Ireland

jurisdictions.name: Scotland
jurisdictions.note: Scottish (devolved) roles for incapacity, death and estate administration, as in force on 2026-09-16. UK-wide roles (DWP appointees, UK GDPR, Access to Health Records Act 1990) are in the uk-national layer.
jurisdictions.label: UK — Scotland

jurisdictions.name: British Columbia
jurisdictions.note: British Columbia provincial roles for incapacity, death and estate administration: enduring and general powers of attorney, representation agreements, temporary substitute decision makers, committees and statutory property guardians, executors and administrators under WESA, organ donation consent, control of disposition of remains, and access to a deceased person's records. Statutes as consolidated on bclaws.gov.bc.ca, current to 15 September 2026 (Supreme Court Civil Rules current to 8 September 2026). Federal roles (CPP/OAS trustees, CRA, PIPEDA, ULCC) are in ca-federal.
jurisdictions.label: Canada — British Columbia

jurisdictions.name: Ontario
jurisdictions.note: Ontario provincial roles for incapacity, death and estates as in force on 2026-09-16 (e-Laws currency date 11 Sept 2026). Federal benefit, tax and privacy roles are in ca-federal.json.
jurisdictions.label: Canada — Ontario

jurisdictions.name: Québec
jurisdictions.note: Québec civil-law roles for incapacity, death and liquidation of successions under the Civil Code of Québec (CCQ) and Code of Civil Procedure (CCP), as amended by S.Q. 2020, c. 11 (in force 1 November 2022). Covers protection mandates, ordinary mandates, assistants, temporary representatives, tutors, consent to care, liquidators, organ donation, funeral arrangements and access to a deceased person's information. Consolidated texts were read from the official LégisQuébec PDFs marked 'Updated to April 7 2026'; later amendments, if any, were not checked. Federal roles are in ca-federal.
jurisdictions.label: Canada — Québec

jurisdictions.name: Mexico — federal law
jurisdictions.note: Código Civil Federal as published by the Cámara de Diputados, last reform DOF 14-11-2025. Mexico is a federation and each state has its own civil code, so succession, capacity and mandate in state matters are governed by state law rather than this one. Organ donation (Ley General de Salud) and disposal of remains are not covered here.
jurisdictions.label: Mexico — federal law

jurisdictions.name: US — uniform/model law + federal
jurisdictions.note: Baseline built from the Uniform Law Commission's model acts (which bind nobody until a state enacts them) plus federal regulations that apply everywhere.
jurisdictions.label: US — uniform/model law + federal

jurisdictions.name: Arizona
jurisdictions.note:
Arizona answers the durability question **twice, and oppositely, inside its own statute book**. A financial power of attorney is durable only if §14-5501(A) is satisfied — the instrument "shall contain words that demonstrate the principal's intent" that the authority survive disability, with two safe-harbour sentences "or similar language" offered in subsection B — and it must additionally be witnessed by a disinterested witness and acknowledged before a notary on the witness's affidavit, or it is not a power at all. A **health care** power of attorney, by contrast, is durable by definition: §36-3201(6) defines it as a designation "that comes into effect and is durable as provided in section 36-3223, subsection A", and nothing has to be said about incapacity. The financial article then seals itself off from health care at §14-5507. Express words required is the majority rule, so that is not a new route to durability; what is new is that **Arizona answers the question oppositely within one statute book** — the same legislature chose opt-in for property and automatic for the body, which makes `poaDurableByDefault` an instrument-level fact here rather than a jurisdiction-level one.

Two other things are distinctive. The power of attorney reaches **past death** more concretely than elsewhere: §36-831(A)(2) names the agent under either a health care or a durable financial power, where that instrument specifically grants disposition authority, as the holder of the duty to make funeral and disposition arrangements — ranked above every blood relative and behind only the spouse — and §36-3221(A) lets one health care power of attorney carry both offices. And §14-3971 is the **widest no-grant route in this data**: $5,000 of wages to a surviving spouse immediately, $200,000 of personal property after 30 days, $300,000 of real property after six months, against the Uniform Probate Code's $25,000. Because §§14-13107 and 14-13108 accept a small-estate affidavit in place of letters, that ceiling is also how wide the no-court path to a custodian's digital-asset disclosure is.

Arizona has a supported decision-making statute (§§14-5721, 14-5722) and it is the sharpest illustration in this reference of what such an agreement is not. §14-5722(G) ends it as a matter of law "at any time the adult becomes an incapacitated person as defined in section 14-5101" and on the appointment of a guardian. A durable power of attorney exists to survive incapacity; Arizona's supported decision-making agreement is void on it, by its own terms.
jurisdictions.label: US — Arizona

jurisdictions.name: Colorado
jurisdictions.note:
Colorado Revised Statutes 2026, title 15 (Probate, Trusts, and Fiduciaries), read from the Office of Legislative Legal Services' own host at olls.info on 14 October 2026. One title is one file there, so every citation's URL is the title and the pinpoint is in the citation text, as with Oklahoma and Delaware.

Colorado is a Uniform Probate Code state, so the roles not patched below — the personal representative, the administrator, the guardian of the person, the RUFADAA fiduciary and the anatomical gift agent — take the us-model baseline. Those sections were not individually re-read for this entry and no claim specific to Colorado is made about them; the article 19 part 2 anatomical gift act is noted as relocated in 2017 on the authority of its own source line and nothing further.

Two things in this jurisdiction are without parallel in the rest of the reference. The durability of a power of attorney is selected by the instrument's creation date, with the superseded magic-words test at §15-14-501 still operative for anything signed before 2010 (§15-14-704(2)). And the small-estate ceiling is not a figure but a formula — twice a CPI-adjusted exempt-property amount keyed to the year of death — so the threshold is recorded as null with the formula in the note rather than as a number this reference has not read from an official source.

Colorado also has a supported decision-making statute (article 14 part 8, §§15-14-801 et seq.) and designated beneficiary agreements (article 22), the latter conferring proxy and surrogate rights that §§15-18.5-103 and 15-18.5-104 both defer to.
jurisdictions.label: US — Colorado

jurisdictions.name: Delaware
jurisdictions.note:
Delaware is the most uniform-act-resistant state in this set on property and succession, and the earliest adopter of the newest uniform act on health care. It has no Uniform Probate Code, no Uniform Trust Code (title 12 chapter 35 is Delaware's own body of trust law), no Uniform Guardianship act beyond the jurisdictional one, and no Revised Uniform Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets Act — yet title 16 chapter 25 is the Uniform Health-Care Decisions Act (2023), in force since 84 Del. Laws c. 467 (2024).

The digital-assets chapter is the reason to read this file. Delaware legislated in 2014, before RUFADAA existed, and never replaced its act: title 12 chapter 50 is the Fiduciary Access to Digital Assets and Digital Accounts Act, seven sections against the uniform act's eighteen, with no online tool and no designated recipient. Its default is the inverse of RUFADAA's — the fiduciary controls everything unless a governing instrument or court order says otherwise — and § 5004 goes further than any other provision in this set by voiding an end-user licence limitation as against the strong public policy of the State and making a choice-of-law clause unenforceable where it would import a law that enforces one.

Two power-of-attorney chapters coexist, but unlike Oklahoma's they divide by purpose rather than by vintage: § 49A-103 sends business and commercial powers, powers coupled with an interest, health-care powers and entity proxies to chapter 49, keeping chapter 49A for personal powers. Chapter 49A borrows the uniform act's numbering and reverses its central rule, § 49A-104 making a power durable only if it says so.

Sourcing note: delcode.delaware.gov is server-rendered and serves a whole chapter per page, so each citation points at the chapter or subchapter page that carries the section quoted; every URL here was checked to contain its section. Larger chapters are split into subchapters and the chapter page is then a few hundred characters of navigation, which is the tell.
jurisdictions.label: US — Delaware

jurisdictions.name: Idaho
jurisdictions.note: Idaho is the first jurisdiction in this set with a live/pending split: title 15 chapter 5 carries two regimes in parallel, the existing protective-proceedings law "[EFFECTIVE UNTIL JANUARY 1, 2027]" and the Uniform Guardianship, Conservatorship, and Other Protective Arrangements Act "[EFFECTIVE JANUARY 1, 2027]", enacted by S 1240 (2026, ch. 79). The guardian and conservator rows record the law in force and carry the pending replacement explicitly. Two other things are worth knowing before reading the patches. adoption.json records no Uniform Probate Code enactment for Idaho, but §15-1-101 says "This act shall be known and may be cited as the uniform probate code", added 1971 ch. 111 — the ULC bill tracker that adoption.json is built from does not reach back to 1971, so it is a false negative here, the opposite of the Pennsylvania UPOAA case. And Idaho enacted no Uniform Health-Care Decisions Act and no Uniform Trust Code: health care runs on the homegrown advance care planning document of title 39 chapter 45, and trusts on the Uniform Probate Code’s article VII in title 15 chapter 7, which is why those two rows differ most from the baseline.
jurisdictions.label: US — Idaho

jurisdictions.name: Indiana
jurisdictions.note:
Indiana is the only jurisdiction in this reference that legislates the **custody of the instrument** rather than only the authority it confers. IC 30-5-11, enacted in 2018, gives the electronic power of attorney a full custodial lifecycle: a designated custodian with twelve statutory duties including commercially reasonable privacy and security, guarding against tampering and keeping different principals' records logically separate (§30-5-11-6); custody transfer on the principal's written instruction, with a delivery receipt that constitutes the successor's acceptance; a thirty-day notice procedure for a custodian that wants out; a duty to deliver the record to the attorney in fact once the principal's death becomes known (§30-5-11-7); and a floor on retention — destruction is permitted only "after the fifth anniversary of the principal's death" (§30-5-11-8). §30-5-11-10 then makes the record prima facie evidence of validity and of the absence of tampering, and extends that presumption "regardless of the number of custodians or other persons who hold, receive, or transfer" it — a chain-of-custody rule, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence — with §30-5-11-9 printing the attestation form that records the chain.

IC 29-1-22 is the other half: a statewide **electronic estate planning documents registry**, taking electronic wills, trust instruments and powers of attorney together with their document integrity evidence, whose index must be "available to the public" and "searchable by digital or online means" free of charge, while the documents themselves stay closed. §29-1-22-2(h) is the part no other jurisdiction here has: on request by any interested person the administrator "shall issue a certified report specifying **whether or not** the registry possesses any items" for a named person — an existence query with a negative answer, which §14 of the findings page records as the thing every other register cannot give. It is **authorised and not established**: §29-1-22-2(a) empowers the supreme court and the office of judicial administration to stand it up "under rules adopted by the Indiana supreme court", and no such rule has been adopted. The Indiana Rules of Court catalogue current as of 1 August 2026 carries 24 rule sets, and a scan of all 743 rule pages — 2,733,977 characters — contains no mention of IC 29-1-22, an electronic will, an electronic trust instrument, document integrity evidence, a complete converted copy or an estate planning documents registry; the only registries in the rules are the ADR commission's mediator registry, the certified interpreter registry and the protection order e-filing registry. Since the statute conditions the registry on rules, their silence answers the question on the statute's own terms. So the one jurisdiction here that legislated a negative-answerable existence endpoint has not switched it on, seven years after P.L.231-2019. And deposit is permissive in any case, so even a running registry would never let absence from it prove absence of a document.

Two further things are Indiana's own. Its refusal remedy is the heaviest in this data: §30-5-9-9 gives a person **three business days** to accept a power of attorney and then imposes **treble damages**, the claimant's attorney's fees and prejudgment interest — the only multiplier anywhere here — and two of its five defences are available only to a refuser that gives the attorney in fact a **written statement of its reason within ten business days**, which makes Indiana the second jurisdiction after Kansas to require a refusal's reasons to be sent somewhere, and the first to send them to the counterparty rather than to a court. And §29-1-8-1(g) wires the small-estate affidavit straight into the digital-assets act: a distributee under the $100,000 affidavit "has the same rights as a personal representative under IC 32-39 to access a digital asset", which is the only route to digital assets in this reference that passes through no court and no letters.

Indiana also closed a channel rather than opening one. §30-5-5-16(e) provides that a document granting health care powers "may not be executed under this chapter after December 31, 2022", and that where a later power grants both health care and other powers "the health care powers are void, but all other powers … remain effective" — partial invalidity rather than a dead instrument. Health care authority now runs through the 2021 advance directive act, IC 16-36-7, whose §34 is a fourteen-item default rule set and whose §44 settles a conflict between documents, including documents signed in other states, in favour of "the document signed last by the declarant".
jurisdictions.label: US — Indiana

jurisdictions.name: Iowa
jurisdictions.note: Iowa is the jurisdiction in this set that most often makes a legal effect turn on **what the relying party knows, or on a clock**, rather than on the instrument. A health-care agent outranks a court-appointed guardian only while “known to the health care provider to be available and willing” (§144B.6(1)); the holder of the right to control a body forfeits it on a murder charge only once “those charges are known to a third party”, and forfeits it outright by not acting within 24 hours of notification or 40 hours of death (§144C.8); an agent’s authority ends when the agent is “named as having abused the principal in a **founded dependent adult abuse report**” — a confidential administrative finding (§633B.110(2)(e)) — while the same registry is what the court must search before appointing a guardian (§633.564). Elsewhere Iowa is the uniform power of attorney act with a mandatory notary and Alternative A, a conservatorship that **suspends and then reinstates** the agency rather than ending or continuing it (§633B.108(2)), a surrogate who can only co-sign with the physician (§144A.7), the only certification of trust with a remedy for refusing it (§633A.4604(6)), and a $50,000 small-estate route that prices refusal and acceptance alike and obliges the custodian to answer whether the estate qualifies (§633.356).
jurisdictions.label: US — Iowa

jurisdictions.name: Kansas
jurisdictions.note: Kansas took no uniform power of attorney act and no uniform probate code, but it did something no other state in this set has yet done: it **replaced its whole guardianship law with the Uniform Guardianship, Conservatorship, and Other Protective Arrangements Act, and that replacement is already in force** — L. 2025, ch. 40, effective 1 January 2026, with §59-3050 now carrying nothing but its repeal note. Idaho is the other UGCOPAA state here and its enactment does not commence until 2027, so the two sit on opposite sides of the same transition. The new act brings two provisions new to this reference: §59-30,123 obliges a third party to recognise a guardian's authority and then requires anyone who refuses to **report the refusal, with reasons, to the court within 10 days**; and §59-30,108 withholds letters of office until the appointee files evidence of completing an instructional programme, and requires every limitation on their powers to be stated on the letters themselves. Elsewhere Kansas is close to Missouri next door — a near-identical magic-words durability test at §58-652, a bonded refusal-of-letters route at §59-2287 — and, like Missouri, it has no default health-care surrogate at all.
jurisdictions.label: US — Kansas

jurisdictions.name: Kentucky
jurisdictions.note: Kentucky was added with West Virginia to read four contiguous states against one uniform act. It is the uniform one on execution — a signature suffices and notarisation buys a presumption — and on the acceptance remedy, where it took Section 120 Alternative A and kept the automatic liability for attorney's fees. It deviates in two places that matter to this reference. A court appointment of a conservator or guardian **terminates** the power of attorney by default (§457.100(1)(c)), the reverse of the uniform act's bracketed rule and of Virginia's enactment of it. And Kentucky has **no monetary threshold at all** for dispensing with administration: §395.470 lets the beneficiaries agree an estate of any size out of administration on unanimous written consent, no debts, taxes provided for and a six-week advertisement at the courthouse door. Its guardianship procedure is also the only one here that is a jury trial by default, with the burden of proof on the Commonwealth. One drafting note for anyone citing it: the ULC bill tracker dates the Uniform Power of Attorney Act enactment to 2020, while §457.010's own history says 2018 Ky. Acts ch. 185, effective 14 July 2018.
jurisdictions.label: US — Kentucky

jurisdictions.name: Louisiana
jurisdictions.note: Louisiana is a civil-law jurisdiction. Roles come from the Civil Code and Code of Civil Procedure, with the Revised Statutes for trusts, anatomical gifts, life-sustaining procedures and disposition of remains. Names do not map onto the common-law model: mandate and mandatary rather than power of attorney and agent, interdiction and curator rather than guardianship and conservatorship, and succession rather than probate.
jurisdictions.label: US — Louisiana

jurisdictions.name: Maine
jurisdictions.note: Maine is the closest state in this set to the uniform baseline: it enacted the Uniform Guardianship, Conservatorship and Other Protective Arrangements Act, the act the us-model baseline follows, and is one of only four states to have done so. Probate law was recodified from Title 18-A to Title 18-C effective 2019, so section numbers in older references are stale.
jurisdictions.label: US — Maine

jurisdictions.name: Maryland
jurisdictions.note: Maryland is on the uniform acts for trusts, digital assets and anatomical gifts and on none of them for powers of attorney, probate or guardianship, and it is the state where the formality of an instrument depends entirely on which instrument it is. A financial power of attorney needs a notary, two witnesses and, if executed remotely, a supervising attorney who certifies what they saw; a health care agent can be appointed by a dated video file with no witnesses, or by speaking in front of a clinician. Two more Maryland particulars matter to this data: the small estate is a simplified administration with letters issued by the register of wills, not a collection by affidavit as in every other US jurisdiction here, and the certification that starts a health care agent's authority requires an examination within the previous two hours.
jurisdictions.label: US — Maryland

jurisdictions.name: Massachusetts
jurisdictions.note: No state-specific disposition-of-remains role: no Massachusetts statute setting a right-of-disposition priority was found, so none is asserted.
jurisdictions.label: US — Massachusetts

jurisdictions.name: Minnesota
jurisdictions.note:
Minnesota's chapter 523, enacted in **1984**, is the most completely worked-out acceptance-and-reliance regime in this data, and it got there two decades before the Uniform Power of Attorney Act. §523.20 makes a party refusing a conforming statutory short form "liable to the principal and to the principal's heirs, assigns, and representative of the estate of the principal **in the same manner as the party would be liable had the party refused to accept the authority of the principal to act on the principal's own behalf**" — word for word the remedy Nebraska is singled out for in §15 of the findings page, except that Nebraska's arrived in 2012 and Minnesota's in 1984. What Minnesota pairs it with is the opposite of Nebraska's: the duty runs only to the **statutory short form** under §523.23 or §523.231, on a six-part conformity checklist, with no seven-day clock and no fee shift. So the narrowest duty in this data carries the strongest remedy, which breaks the last link §15 had left between an instrument's formality and the obligation it attracts. Minnesota also goes past reliance to **conclusive proof**: §§523.16 and 523.17 make an agent's affidavit conclusive as to a relying party, where the rest of this set offers permission to rely absent actual knowledge.

Two further things are Minnesota's own. It has **no default health-care surrogate**, which makes it the third US jurisdiction here without one — and the first where a statute says so rather than being silent: §145B.12 provides that where no living will was executed "a presumption is not created" about the individual's intentions or the appropriate care. And §149A.80 **expressly excludes the power of attorney** from the class of written instruments that can appoint someone to control disposition of remains, reasoning from its own §§523.08 and 523.09 termination rule — the precise inverse of Arizona's §36-831(A)(2), which names the durable-power agent as a holder of that duty.

The durability rule itself is ordinary: §523.07 is express-words opt-in with a purposive "or similar words" test, and §523.01 makes notarisation a condition of valid execution. §523.11 then keeps the pre-uniform rule that a conservator **or guardian** holds the principal's own power to "revoke, suspend, or terminate all or any part" of the instrument — with suspension and partial revocation, which the other states holding that rule do not have.
jurisdictions.label: US — Minnesota

jurisdictions.name: Missouri
jurisdictions.note: Missouri took neither the Uniform Power of Attorney Act nor the Uniform Probate Code nor any uniform health-care decisions act, and the result is the most distinctive state in this set. Two things run through it. First, **it answers the relying party's problem with security rather than with duty**: no statute obliges anyone to accept a Missouri power of attorney and none shifts fees on refusal, but §404.719(4) lets the third person demand indemnity against forgery by bond, §456.10-1013(2) lets it require a certification of trust to be acknowledged or guaranteed and signed by every trustee, and the small-estate and refusal-of-letters routes at §§473.097 and 473.090 both require the claimant to post a bond. Second, **formality is loaded onto creation and almost absent from revocation**: §404.705 makes a durable power valid only if it is titled as one, recites one of two capitalised statutory sentences and is acknowledged as if it conveyed land, while §404.850 lets the health-care version be revoked "in any manner by which the patient is able to communicate" and §404.717 lets the financial version be terminated orally. Missouri is also the only US jurisdiction here with **no default health-care surrogate** at all.
jurisdictions.label: US — Missouri

jurisdictions.name: Nebraska
jurisdictions.note: Nebraska is the most uniform-law state in this set — the probate code, the power of attorney act, the trust code, the digital-assets act and the anatomical gift act are all the uniform texts, and its trust-code catchlines even print the uniform section numbers. That makes its two departures unusually legible. It **kept the rule the Uniform Power of Attorney Act was written to abolish**: §30-4008(2) gives a court-appointed conservator the principal's own power to revoke or amend the power of attorney, which the official comment to uniform §108 identifies as the pre-2006 position the section departs from. And it **omitted Section 1013**, so Nebraska is the only Uniform Trust Code state here whose successor trustee has no statutory certification of trust to produce. Against those, §30-4020 builds the strongest duty to accept a power of attorney in this data, adding prohibited grounds for refusal and a liability rule equating refusal of the agent with refusal of the principal; and the 2018 Health Care Surrogacy Act lets a person appoint a surrogate merely by telling their clinician. The adoption tracker records no Uniform Probate Code enactment for Nebraska, which is a false negative of the Idaho kind — §30-2601 calls it the Nebraska Probate Code.
jurisdictions.label: US — Nebraska

jurisdictions.name: Oklahoma
jurisdictions.note:
Oklahoma is **not** a Uniform Probate Code state: title 58 is its own Probate Procedure code, descended from the 1910 Revised Laws, and the grant is named for the appointee's capacity — letters testamentary for an executor (§ 58-110), letters of administration for an administrator (§ 58-121), each with a statutory form whose date line still reads “A. D., 19__”. The uniform acts Oklahoma has adopted were layered on top and in unexpected places: the Uniform Power of Attorney Act went into title 58 at § 3001 rather than title 15 with the older power-of-attorney law, and the digital-assets act into the same title at § 3101. Two power-of-attorney regimes now coexist with opposite durability defaults, which § 58-3003 resolves by applying the 2021 act to all powers of attorney bar four carve-outs.

Health care is the live question. The Oklahoma Health Care Agent Act (§ 63-3111.1, 2022) and the Advance Directive Act govern today, backed by a State Department of Health registry that stores directives and gives named agents access to them (§ 63-3102.1). Enrolled HB 1687 (2026) creates a Uniform Health Care Decisions Act of 2026, repeals the Health Care Agent Act and introduces a default surrogate — and provides that “this act shall become effective July 1, 2027”. It is therefore enacted and not in force, and this file records the law as it stands with the replacement marked pending.

Sourcing note: Oklahoma publishes its consolidated statutes only as whole-title PDFs at oklegislature.gov/OK_Statutes/CompleteTitles/, which is what every statute citation here points to and what was read. Those files are a 31 December 2025 snapshot, so nothing enacted in the 2026 session appears in them; the 2026 act is cited to its enrolled bill instead. OSCN, which publishes section-by-section pages, sits behind a Cloudflare Turnstile and was not used.
jurisdictions.label: US — Oklahoma

jurisdictions.name: Utah
jurisdictions.note: Utah recodified in three steps, and the section numbers in any older reference are stale. Title 75 remains the Utah Uniform Probate Code (estates, guardianship and conservatorship, and since 2025 a supported decision-making part). Effective 1 September 2024, Laws 2024 ch. 364 created title 75A, “Fiduciaries”, and moved the Uniform Power of Attorney Act into 75A-2 and the digital-assets act into 75A-6; the Advance Health Care Directive Act was renumbered out of 75-2a on the same date. Title 75B, “Trusts”, took the Uniform Trust Code, and old title 75 chapter 7 was repealed outright on 7 May 2025. The anatomical gift act moved again in the 2023 health-code recodification and is now title 26B chapter 8 part 3. On top of that Utah enacted a new Uniform Health Care Decisions Act in 2025 (Laws 2025 ch. 439, title 75A chapter 9), whose transitional section keys the chapter to 1 January 2026; it is the only jurisdiction in this set on a Uniform Health Care Decisions Act of that generation rather than the 1993 act or home-grown law. Existence of a section was confirmed from the legislature's XML for each title rather than from a page load: le.utah.gov renders statutes client-side and answers 200 with a URL-derived <title> for sections that do not exist.
jurisdictions.label: US — Utah

jurisdictions.name: Virginia
jurisdictions.note: Virginia is the uniform-act neighbour of a non-uniform state, and the contrast is the point of adding it. It took the Uniform Power of Attorney Act with its numbering and its durability default intact where Delaware took the numbering and inverted the default; it repealed its own early digital-assets act and adopted RUFADAA where Delaware kept its own; and it is on the Uniform Trust Code and the Revised Uniform Anatomical Gift Act where Delaware is on neither. Where Virginia is unusual it is unusual about time: a seven-business-day deadline to accept a power of attorney, a finding of incapacity that must be re-certified every 180 days, guardianship review hearings within a year and then every three years, a 60-day wait for the small-estate affidavit, and two sections of the guardianship chapter printed in two versions whose switchover is contingent rather than dated.
jurisdictions.label: US — Virginia

jurisdictions.name: West Virginia
jurisdictions.note: West Virginia was added with Kentucky to test what happens when four contiguous states — Virginia, West Virginia, Maryland and Kentucky — are read against one uniform act, and it turned out to be the most consistently non-standard of them. It is the only one of the four that makes acknowledgement a condition of a power of attorney's validity rather than a presumption of genuineness; the only one that softened Uniform Power of Attorney Act §120's automatic liability for attorney's fees into a judicial discretion; and, with Kentucky, one of two that reversed §108(b)'s bracketed rule so that appointing a conservator terminates the agency by default. Separately, article 44-3A makes the office that supervises estate administration a **county** choice rather than a state one, which is sub-state variation of a kind nothing else in this data records.
jurisdictions.label: US — West Virginia

jurisdictions.name: New South Wales
jurisdictions.note: NSW state roles as in force on 2026-09-16; Commonwealth nominee, My Health Record, tax and Privacy Act features are in au-commonwealth.
jurisdictions.label: Australia — New South Wales

jurisdictions.name: Queensland
jurisdictions.note: Queensland state law on enduring documents, statutory health attorneys, QCAT appointments, deceased estates, tissue donation and cremation, as in force on 2026-09-16 (reprints current as at 28 April 2026 for the main Acts). Commonwealth roles are in the au-commonwealth layer.
jurisdictions.label: Australia — Queensland

jurisdictions.name: Victoria
jurisdictions.note: Victorian state law on substitute and supported decision-making, deceased estates, tissue donation and disposal of remains, as in force on 2026-09-16. Commonwealth roles (Centrelink, My Health Record, ATO, Privacy Act) are in the au-commonwealth layer.
jurisdictions.label: Australia — Victoria

jurisdictions.name: Argentina
jurisdictions.note: Roles from the Código Civil y Comercial de la Nación (Ley 26.994). Argentina answers impaired capacity with support measures first and curatorship only for incapacity, and has no durable financial power: the mandate ends on the incapacity of either party, while health directives may be made expressly in anticipation of incapacity. Succession vests without a grant. The separate transplant statute (Ley 27.447) was not retrieved, so only the Code’s body-donation rule is recorded.
jurisdictions.label: Argentina

jurisdictions.name: Brazil
jurisdictions.note: Brazilian federal law: Código Civil (Lei nº 10.406/2002) as consolidated by the Presidência da República, including the changes made by the Estatuto da Pessoa com Deficiência (Lei nº 13.146/2015). Organ donation under Lei nº 9.434/1997 and the disposal of remains are not covered here.
jurisdictions.label: Brazil
